## Question 3
**Answer: True.** `lst[[2]]` is `population`, which is itself a list, so `[[ ]]` returns a list.
Source: Class 04 deck "[ ] vs [[ ]] on a List"; Class 05 deck "One Table for Three Brackets"; your class04.Rmd lines 69-74 and class05.Rmd lines 25-31.
```{r question_3}
lst = list(
  gdp = data.frame(year = c(2020, 2021, 2022), values = c(19200, 20500, 21300), units = "USD billions"),
  population = list(country = "United States", year = c(2020, 2021, 2022), values = c(325, 331, 335), units = "millions"),
  indicators = c("gdp", "population", "inflation"),
  inflation_rate = 3.2
)
class(lst[[2]])   # "list" -> True
```

## Question 7 
```{r question_7}
library(httr2); library(rvest)
robotstxt::paths_allowed('https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami_University')

pt = request('https://api.weather.gov/points/26.1420,-81.7948') |> req_user_agent('student isa401') |> req_perform() |> resp_body_json()
str(pt$properties[c('gridId','gridX','gridY')])   # MFL, 45, 60
for (p in c('26.1420,-81.7948','26.1167,-81.7954','26.17,-81.77')) {x = request(paste0('https://api.weather.gov/points/', p)) |> req_user_agent('student isa401') |> req_perform() |> resp_body_json(); cat(p, x$properties$gridId, x$properties$gridX, x$properties$gridY, '\n')}   # 45/60, 45/59, 46/61
```
**Answer: True** (paths_allowed returned TRUE, RAN). Source: Class 10 deck "The Scraping Workflow" and "Check Three Sites"; your class10.Rmd lines 23-60.

## Question 9 
```{r question_9}
tabs = read_html('https://miamiredhawks.com/sports/swimming-and-diving/roster') |>
  html_elements('table') |>
  html_table()


women = tabs[[1]][-1, c(1, 3)]; names(women) = c('name', 'academic year')
men   = tabs[[2]][-1, c(1, 3)]; names(men)   = c('name', 'academic year')
swim_df = dplyr::bind_rows(women, men)
dim(swim_df)   # 54 x 2 (RAN with column 4 = location)
```
**Answer: 54 rows x 2 columns** (name plus a second column; RAN). The roster page has 3 tables (Women, Men, Coaching); the first row of each is the real header, so `[-1, ]` drops it. Your version uses column 3 (academic year) because the requirement says "names and years"; the first line of the question says location (column 4 in my run). Check `tabs[[1]]` to confirm the columns. Source: Class 10 deck "All the Tables on a Wikipedia Page"; Class 11 deck and your class_11_complete.Rmd lines 101-109; `[-1, c(1, 3)]` brackets: Class 05 deck "One Table for Three Brackets".

## Question 11
**Answer: `ip_df`, 10 rows x 17 columns.** One IP was RUN (1 x 17); the 10-IP loop was NOT run because toxic_ips_oct2025.csv was never provided. Source: Class 11 deck (purrr::map_df, .x and .f); Class 08 deck "A Request, Step by Step"; your class_11_complete.Rmd line 89 and hw07.Rmd lines 79-113.
```{r question_11, eval=FALSE}
library(httr2)
ip_api = 'status,continent,country,countryCode,region,regionName,city,district,zip,lat,lon,timezone,currency,isp,org,as,query'

get_ip = function(ip) {
  request(paste0('http://ip-api.com/json/', ip)) |>
    req_url_query(fields = ip_api) |>
    req_perform() |>
    resp_body_string() |>
    jsonlite::fromJSON() |>
    as.data.frame()
}

ips = readr::read_csv('toxic_ips_oct2025.csv')[[1]]
length(ips)   # must be 10; if 9, the file has no header: use read_csv(..., col_names = FALSE)
ip_df = purrr::map_df(ips, function(x) { Sys.sleep(0.5); get_ip(x) })
dim(ip_df)    # target: 10 x 17
```

## Question 12
**Answer: probably "neither tidy nor consistent" - UNVERIFIED GUESS** (I could not open the file). Run glimpse first. Tidy = one variable per column, one observation per row, one value per cell (years across the top means not tidy). In Class 13, "consistent" means missing and impossible values (named, not taught). Source: Class 13 deck "Technically Correct Data" and the tidy rules.

```{r question_12, eval=FALSE}
wb_tbl = readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fmegahed/isa401/main/data/wb_hospital_beds.csv')
```


## Question 14
**Answer: not technically correct.** `id`, `hbcu_indicator` and `carnegie_category` are codes stored as numbers (should be text). read_csv already trims the spaces in ` endowment_fy_20 `, so the name needed no fix in my run (RAN). Source: Class 13 deck "Technically Correct Data" (reasonable names + correct types).
```{r question_14}
sapply(ntse_tbl, class)
ntse_tbl = ntse_tbl |>
  dplyr::mutate(id = as.character(id),
                hbcu_indicator = as.character(hbcu_indicator),
                carnegie_category = as.character(carnegie_category))
sapply(ntse_tbl, class)
```

## Question 15
**Answer (draft, my wording; edit freely):**

- R scripts are repeatable: rerunning the same code gives the same result, unlike manual spreadsheet steps that are easy to break.
- Code can pull data from APIs, scraped pages and JSON files that spreadsheets cannot reach easily.
- Cleaning, analysis and charts live in one workflow, so changes flow through everything automatically.
- Version control (Git) tracks every change to the code, so mistakes can be undone and work shared.
- Scripts are readable and reusable on new data, while spreadsheet errors are hard to spot.

Source: Class 02 deck "Spreadsheets That Made the News" and "Learning Objectives".
